Wait, why do we hate systemd again?

I honestly don't mind it, although I see why some do:

Most upfront is that it flies in the face of the biggest Linux ideal, where you have a lot of little packages that do one thing very well. Systemd, on the other hand, does a lot of things, and they often fail because they're not made to be one giant package. It keeps absorbing things for no apparent reason, and that's not very Linux-y.

Second, it stores all logs in binary instead of the standard ASCII text. This means that, if you have any data corruption to your logs you will lose the entire log instead of just the corrupted portion.

Finally, systemd seems to be strong-arming their way into our lives... again flying in the face of the Linux ideal of having choices. It's mandatory if you want Gnome, it's mandatory if you want to use most distros, and it's forcing its influence into more and more places daily. You'd actually have a hard time finding a distro that doesn't run systemd these days, which is a shame.

But there are also good things to systemd:

It's fast... like really, really fast. Boot times are much faster than traditional init systems.

It works (for the most part). Yes, there are times when parts of systemd don't work, but I have never personally been faced with one of these instances. It's always worked just fine for me, and I can't complain about that.

Systemd incorporates so many things that I usually don't have to add packages to it in order to make my system work. I don't need Grub, since systemd absorbed Gummiboot. I don't need networkmanager since systemd has netctl included. And the list goes on and on. Some see this as bloat, and it is... but it's also convenient.

So, is it bad? Yes.

But is it also good? I think so.

I can see where people would dislike systemd, and I tend to agree with them. But I'm also not going to compile my own distro, so there's not much room for me to complain.
